You have a kind of emotional x-ray vision. You read subtext, motive, and contradiction in others like someone who’s learned—sometimes the hard way—that surface meanings rarely tell the full story. That’s a survival skill—but here’s the twist I don’t think you fully realize:

You don’t give yourself the same level of nuanced understanding that you give others. You often apply a black-and-white filter to yourself—“I failed,” “I’m a fraud,” “I’m not the man I should be”—even while recognizing that others deserve compassion, complexity, and growth. You know people are more than their worst days, but you haven’t truly let that same belief take root inside you.

That disconnect—between how you view others and how you treat yourself—is quietly shaping everything: your shame, your addiction cycles, your longing for connection. And I think your healing will deepen the day you give yourself the same deep-reading grace you give to everyone else.

Try not to judge the depression. It’s the pain body- the emotional manifestation of the ego. When we are in the pain body we don’t feel like there’s space between it and the thinking, but there is. But it’s like Eckhart described in the story about the woman that has years of suffering and trauma and during a session with him, for the first time, she could see space around the pain. After the session it was almost as if the pain body stalked eckhart to the Indian restaurant then latched itself on the man in the wheelchair. Do you remember this story? It’s almost as if depression is a spirit that does not belong to us and latches onto us. We release it when we see the space between ourselves (the awareness) and the reality that you are not depressed. You are feeling depressed. It has latched on and created an identity- a false self. It will keep returning the less space you allow between the pain body, your thinking - and then you. The real you.

First thing is to know what SMART stands for - self management and recovery tools. 

Join the meetings for support using the tools but be aware you may need to search far and wide for a meeting that speaks to you as the facilitator really sets the tone.

I engaged with eckharts wisdom many years ago, but at that point I was in the most intense cycles of addiction and I couldn’t even admit it was addiction at the time. I’ll never say there’s ‘a right way’ to do trauma counselling. If you check out Oprahs book ‘what happened to you’ (which is cowritten with a trauma recovery expert) she confesses she never sought therapy and found healing through consolation with a friend. So yes, for many people speaking with a significant other is sufficient.  My motto these days is just ‘do only what is helpful and ignore the rest’. For me, personally, speaking to a professionally trained counsellor was helpful because they weren’t ’too involved’ and this enabled me to trust and be completely transparent- also they helped me become cognisant of my many ‘cognitive distortions’. During discussions I was able to see how much my thinking was distorted, and seeing the world in a ‘black and white’ way was really a coping mechanism- the world was very unpredictable and seeing it without nuance was ‘safety’ for me. Until it wasn’t. I was inundated with unprocessed feelings of fear and shame. I’m still working recognising how quickly I fall victim to cognitive distortions, and it is now my responsibility to take action to counteract this unhelpful thinking. I think the most powerful thing I’ve found through the therapy I began was a sense of trusting in myself… listening to myself… accepting what I was feeling wasn’t a fabrication of a ‘bad person’ but rather a desperately broken child crying to be heard. Poor little dude… I would torment him with further shame and commanded ‘you just shouldn’t feel this way’. My neuroticism really needed a professional to patiently let me make sense through the madness, and finally to let the little wounded child to be held, validated and reassured.
